s: The Oxydracee and Mallii were prepared with an army of more than eighty thousand foot, ten thousand horse, and seven hundred chariots. Instead of confronting Alexander in the open field, their forces withdrew into neighboring cities after disputes over supreme command.

s: While Alexander recovered from his wound, about three thousand Greek colonists in Bactria and Sogdiana rebelled, but all were killed after his death. Alexander then held a feast, where Dioxippus defeated Coragus in a duel, was later falsely accused of theft, and killed himself. Alexander continued down the Indus, receiving submissions and conquering territories, including those of the Brachmanes, before beginning the siege of Harmatelia. During fighting near Harmatelia, Ptolemy was poisoned but was healed after Alexander found an effective herb in a dream.

l: Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, In the mean time, while the king lay ill of his wound, the Gft-
s: Alexander recovered from his wound, offered a solemn sacrifice, and feasted his friends. He favored Coragus in the duel but later became troubled by Dioxippus's death and praised his valor. He led his army and fleet down the Indus, received submissions, conquered several territories, and began the siege of Harmatelia. After Ptolemy was wounded by poisoned weapons, Alexander dreamed of a healing herb, found it, and used it to restore Ptolemy and others.

l: Macedonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, In the mean time, while the king lay ill of his wound, the Gft-
s: The Macedonians favored Coragus during his duel with Dioxippus. Alexander led them along the bank of the Indus, where they received submissions and conquered or destroyed several Indian cities.

l: Coragus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, In the mean time, while the king lay ill of his wound, the Gft-
s: Coragus was a strong Macedonian soldier who had fought gallantly in earlier encounters. After challenging Dioxippus, he was defeated, knocked down, and briefly held beneath Dioxippus's foot before Alexander ordered him released.

l: Dioxippus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, In the mean time, while the king lay ill of his wound, the Gft-
s: Dioxippus was an Athenian champion who had won many prizes and victories. He defeated Coragus in the duel, but later faced a false accusation of theft and killed himself after writing to Alexander.

l: duel between Coragus and Dioxippus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, In the mean time, while the king lay ill of his wound, the Gft-
s: In the duel, Coragus appeared armed while Dioxippus fought naked with a club. Dioxippus avoided Coragus's javelin, broke his sarissa, prevented him from drawing his sword, and knocked him down; Alexander then ordered Coragus released.

l: Dioxippus's false theft accusation, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, In the mean time, while the king lay ill of his wound, the Gft-
s: The king's friends and courtiers arranged for a golden cup to be placed under Dioxippus's cushion. During a feast they accused him of stealing it, and the cup was supposedly found with him, disgracing him and causing him to leave the table.

l: Dioxippus's suicide, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, In the mean time, while the king lay ill of his wound, the Gft-
s: After leaving the feast, Dioxippus wrote to Alexander accusing his enemies of plotting against him. Once he had given the letter to his servants for delivery, he killed himself; Alexander later regretted his death and recognized the honesty of Dioxippus through the knavery of his accusers.

l: Indus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, In the mean time, while the king lay ill of his wound, the Gft-
s: Alexander ordered his army to march along the bank of the Indus while his fleet sailed down the river toward the ocean. The Sogdiani and Massanii bordered both sides of the river, and Sambus escaped across it with thirty elephants.

l: Brachmanes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, In the mean time, while the king lay ill of his wound, the Gft-
s: The Brachmanes suffered Alexander's campaigns after revolting following their submission. Alexander destroyed or enslaved inhabitants of many cities in their territories and put more than eighty thousand barbarians to the sword, while pardoning most others who submitted.

l: Harmatelia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, In the mean time, while the king lay ill of his wound, the Gft-
s: Harmatelia was described as the last city attacked among the Brachmanes. Its inhabitants trusted in their own valor and the strength of its position, but ultimately came out, begged Alexander's pardon, and surrendered themselves and their city.

l: siege of Harmatelia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, In the mean time, while the king lay ill of his wound, the Gft-
s: Before the siege, Alexander used a feigned retreat to draw three thousand inhabitants of Harmatelia into battle. The defenders used deadly snake poison on their weapons, causing severe suffering and death among the wounded, but the inhabitants later surrendered when Alexander began the siege.

l: Ptolemy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, In the mean time, while the king lay ill of his wound, the Gft-
s: Ptolemy was greatly loved for his valor and obliging behavior. He was wounded by a poisoned weapon during the fighting near Harmatelia and was believed to be in desperate danger, but Alexander's treatment restored him to perfect health.

l: Ptolemy's healing, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, In the mean time, while the king lay ill of his wound, the Gft-
s: Alexander dreamed that a serpent showed him an herb and explained its nature and location. He found the herb, applied it as a poultice, and gave Ptolemy its juice as a potion, curing Ptolemy and later other wounded men.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Then sailing with his familiar friends into the main ocean, he
s: Alexander sailed into the main ocean, explored islands, returned up the river, and sent Nearchus and others to survey the sea-coast to the Euphrates. He marched through Gedrosia and neighboring regions, dividing his army into brigades, suffering severe losses during a desert crossing, and eventually reaching Carmania and then Susa. At Susa he married Statira, arranged other marriages, received thirty thousand trained Persians, and dealt with the misconduct of his governors and the mutiny of the Macedonians. The unit also recounts Calanus's self-immolation and Harpalus's corruption, flight, and death.

l: Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Then sailing with his familiar friends into the main ocean, he
s: Alexander sailed with his familiar friends into the main ocean, offered sacrifices, and returned with the fleet up the river to Hyala. He marched through Gedrosia and other territories, dividing his army into three brigades and subduing or destroying the inhabitants. He later reached Susa, married Statira, arranged marriages for his friends, received thirty thousand trained Persians, punished corrupt governors, and confronted the mutiny of the Macedonians.

l: Hyala, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Then sailing with his familiar friends into the main ocean, he
s: Hyala was a famous city governed like Lacedaemon, with two hereditary kings responsible for war and a senate holding chief authority in civil affairs. Alexander reached it after returning up the river, repaired or burned his defective ships there, and entrusted the remaining fleet to Nearchus and others.

l: Alexander's fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Then sailing with his familiar friends into the main ocean, he
s: Alexander's fleet sailed into the main ocean and reached two islands where magnificent sacrifices were offered. At Hyala, defective ships were burned, while the remaining ships were placed under Nearchus and other friends to explore the sea-coast to the entrance of the river Euphrates.

l: Euphrates, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Then sailing with his familiar friends into the main ocean, he
s: The river Euphrates was the intended endpoint of the sea-coast exploration undertaken by Nearchus and the other commanders of Alexander's fleet. After hearing their report, Alexander ordered the fleet to sail to the Euphrates.

l: Gedrosia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Then sailing with his familiar friends into the main ocean, he
s: Alexander marched through Gedrosia and brought its inhabitants to submission without hazard or difficulty. He later marched through Gedrosia along the sea-coast, passing among savage peoples and then through a barren wilderness.

l: desert crossing, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Then sailing with his familiar friends into the main ocean, he
s: During the desert crossing, Alexander's army passed through waterless tracts and a wilderness lacking all support for human life. Many soldiers died from hunger, and mountaineers later attacked Leonatus's squadron, causing another loss.

l: Alexander's army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Then sailing with his familiar friends into the main ocean, he
s: Alexander divided his army into three brigades under Ptolemy, Leonatus, and himself, assigning them to the sea-coast, the inland country, and the mountainous regions. The army suffered heavily from famine and attacks during the desert crossing, then rested in a rich country and celebrated a seven-day feast to Bacchus.

l: sea-coast exploration, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Then sailing with his familiar friends into the main ocean, he
s: Nearchus and other friends were ordered to sail along the sea-coast, observe every place carefully, and continue to the entrance of the river Euphrates. They later reported extraordinary tides, submerged islands, fierce winds, and whales of incredible size.

l: Calanus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Then sailing with his familiar friends into the main ocean, he
s: Calanus was an Indian philosopher honored by Alexander. At the age of seventy-three, after becoming ill, he requested permission to end his life on a funeral pile and was consumed by fire; Alexander ordered him to be honorably buried.

l: Calanus's self-immolation, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Then sailing with his familiar friends into the main ocean, he
s: Calanus's self-immolation occurred when he ascended a funeral pile and was burned with it, following his own philosophical convictions. Some witnesses judged the act madness or vanity, while others admired his courage and contempt for death.

l: Susa, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Then sailing with his familiar friends into the main ocean, he
s: At Susa, Alexander married Statira, the eldest daughter of Darius, and married Drypetis to Hephestion. He also arranged marriages between his leading friends and Persian noblewomen, received thirty thousand trained Persians, and later dealt with the Macedonian mutiny.

l: thirty thousand Persians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Then sailing with his familiar friends into the main ocean, he
s: Thirty thousand young Persian men, trained in martial discipline and equipped with Macedonian arms, came to Susa. They demonstrated their skill before Alexander and received large and rich gifts; Alexander intended them to serve as a curb upon the Macedonian phalanx.

l: Macedonian phalanx, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Then sailing with his familiar friends into the main ocean, he
s: The Macedonian phalanx was to be checked by the thirty thousand trained Persians. Alexander sought this balance because the Macedonians had refused to cross the Ganges and had opposed and mocked him in their assembly.

l: Macedonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Then sailing with his familiar friends into the main ocean, he
s: The Macedonians rejoiced when the fleet returned from its sea voyage, filling the theatre with acclamations. Later they refused to cross the Ganges, opposed Alexander in assembly, and mutinied when he appointed Persians to chief commands; they eventually sought to regain his favor with petitions and tears.

l: Harpalus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Then sailing with his familiar friends into the main ocean, he
s: Harpalus, Alexander's treasurer and governor of Babylon, abused his authority during Alexander's Indian expedition by indulging in luxury, sexual misconduct, extravagant provisions, and lavish gifts to Pythonice and Glycera. Fearing punishment after Alexander punished corrupt governors, he fled Asia with five thousand talents and six thousand mercenaries, sought protection from the Athenians, and was later murdered in Crete by Thimbron.

l: Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Then sailing with his familiar friends into the main ocean, he
s: Harpalus sought protection from Athens and distributed large rewards among orators who managed his case. After examining the money he had given, the Athenians condemned Demosthenes and several other orators for accepting his bribes.

l: Macedonian mutiny, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Then sailing with his familiar friends into the main ocean, he
s: The Macedonian mutiny grew from the soldiers' opposition to Alexander and their resentment of Persian appointments to chief commands. Alexander seized some leaders and delivered them to the lictors for execution, after which the Macedonians sought reconciliation through petitions and tears.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. XI.
s: Alexander reorganizes his forces by appointing Persians as body squires and incorporating Persian darters and slingers among his soldiers. He marches from Susa through Media, visits Bagistame, reaches Ecbatana, and mourns the death of Hephaestion. While Alexander is in Asia, unrest in Greece produces the Lamian War, as discharged mercenary soldiers and Persian commanders gather at Tenarus under Leosthenes. Alexander then conquers the Cussaei, marches toward Babylon, temporarily avoids the city because of a warning from the Chaldeans, and finally enters it after philosophers persuade him to disregard their astrology.

l: Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. XI.
s: Alexander appointed Persians to replace dismissed men and selected a thousand Persians as body squires. He marched from Susa through Media, conquered the Cussaei in forty days, and proceeded toward Babylon. After initially turning aside because of a Chaldean warning, he accepted philosophical arguments against divination and entered Babylon with his army.

l: Persians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. XI.
s: Alexander appointed Persians to fill the places of men he had discharged and chose a thousand of them as body squires. Peucestes later brought twenty thousand Persian darters and slingers, whom Alexander intermixed with the other soldiers. Persian governors and commanders also gathered forces at Tenarus during the disturbances in Greece.

l: Macedonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. XI.
s: Alexander believed that the Persians appointed as body squires could be trusted as safely as the Macedonians. Some Macedonians had sons by captives; Alexander found ten thousand such sons and appointed instructors to educate them.

l: Alexander's army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. XI.
s: Alexander's army was reorganized by mixing Persian darters and slingers among the other soldiers, bringing it into a condition of ready obedience. It marched from Susa through Media, rested at several places, and later entered Babylon, where the soldiers were entertained by the citizens and enjoyed abundant provisions.

l: Ecbatana, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. XI.
s: Ecbatana in Media was a city two hundred and fifty furlongs in compass and the metropolis of Media, where much treasure was stored. Alexander rested his army there and spent time in feasting, drinking, and stage-plays.

l: Media, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. XI.
s: Alexander marched through Media after leaving Susa and later reached Ecbatana, its metropolis. The Cussaei inhabited the hilly and mountainous parts of Media.

l: Hephaestion, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. XI.
s: Hephaestion, whom Alexander loved above all others, became sick from a surfeit and died at Ecbatana. Alexander was greatly grieved and entrusted his body to Perdiccas to carry to Babylon for an elaborate burial.

l: Greece, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. XI.
s: While Alexander was occupied in Asia, Greece was filled with tumults and seditions. These disturbances led to the war called the Lamian War.

l: Asia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. XI.
s: During Alexander's activities in Asia, discharged mercenary soldiers wandered through the region, robbing and spoiling the country for lack of subsistence. Persian governors and commanders also assembled men and money there before joining the forces at Tenarus.

l: Lamian War, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. XI.
s: The Lamian War broke out after Alexander ordered the provincial governors to disband all mercenary soldiers. Discharged foreigners gathered at Tenarus, where they joined with Persian forces and made Leosthenes their general.

l: mercenary soldiers, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. XI.
s: After being discharged under the king's order, many mercenary soldiers wandered through Asia without subsistence and robbed and spoiled the country. They eventually gathered together at Tenarus in Laconia.

l: Tenarus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. XI.
s: Tenarus in Laconia was the place where discharged mercenary soldiers gathered. Persian governors and commanders brought additional men and money there, and the combined forces appointed Leosthenes as their general.

l: Leosthenes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. XI.
s: Leosthenes, an Athenian described as brave-spirited, was made general of the forces assembled at Tenarus. He convened a council of war, distributed fifty talents to pay the mercenaries, secured arms, and sent ambassadors to the Aetolians seeking their support.

l: Cussaei, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. XI.
s: The Cussaei were a very warlike people inhabiting the mountainous parts of Media who had never been subdued during the Persian empire. Alexander defeated them in repeated engagements, captured many of them, and compelled them to submit and promise future loyalty and obedience.

l: Cussae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. XI.
s: Alexander first seized the passes into the country of Cussae and ravaged much of it. After overcoming its defenders and taking many prisoners, he built cities at the most difficult passes before marching away.

l: conquest of the Cussaei, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. XI.
s: Alexander's conquest of the Cussaei lasted forty days. He secured the passes, defeated the inhabitants, forced them to surrender their liberty for the preservation of their country, and established cities at difficult points.

l: Babylon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. XI.
s: Alexander marched toward Babylon after conquering the Cussaei. He initially camped two hundred furlongs away after hearing a Chaldean warning, but later entered Babylon with his army, where the citizens welcomed the soldiers and provisions were abundant.

l: Chaldeans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. XI.
s: The Chaldeans were famous for astrology and believed they could foresee that Alexander would die soon after entering Babylon. They sent Belephants to warn him and urged him to avoid the city and rebuild the sepulchre of Belus, but Alexander ultimately disregarded their warning.

l: astrology, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. XI.
s: The Chaldeans used astrology to prognosticate future events by observing the stars. Their astrologers predicted Alexander's death after entering Babylon, but philosophical arguments persuaded him to despise divination, especially that of the Chaldeans.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. XII. /
s: Ambassadors from many regions came to Alexander to congratulate him, offer gifts, make alliances, settle accusations, or oppose the restoration of exiles. Alexander arranged an immense funeral for Hephaestion, costing more than twelve thousand talents, and ordered sacrifices to him as a demigod. Numerous prodigies were interpreted as signs of Alexander’s approaching death, and he died after a severe illness, having reigned twelve years and seven months. Some writers attributed his death to poisoning arranged by Antipater, while Darius’s mother, Sysigambis, died of grief and hunger five days later.

l: Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. XII. /
s: Alexander received ambassadors from nearly all parts of the world and gave them favorable answers. He arranged Hephaestion’s funeral on an extraordinary scale, later suffered a severe illness, and died after ruling for twelve years and seven months. Before his death, he gave his ring to Perdiccas and said that he left the kingdom to the most deserving.

l: Hephaestion, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. XII. /
s: Hephaestion was Alexander’s most intimate friend, whom Alexander distinguished by saying that Craterus was the king’s friend but Hephaestion was Alexander’s friend. After Hephaestion died, Alexander honored him with an immense funeral and ordered sacrifices to him as a demigod.

l: Hephaestion's funeral, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. XII. /
s: Alexander arranged Hephaestion’s funeral with greater pomp than any earlier funeral and intended it never to be surpassed. Commanders, soldiers, ambassadors, and inhabitants contributed to it, and its cost exceeded twelve thousand talents.

l: Alexander's death, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. XII. /
s: Alexander died after a violent illness that followed a banquet at which he drank from the great bowl called Hercules’s cup. His final words foretold that his chief friends and commanders would fight and contend over his funeral.

l: ambassadors to Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. XII. /
s: Ambassadors came to Alexander from almost every part of the world. They came to congratulate him, offer crowns and gifts, make leagues and alliances, clear themselves of accusations, or oppose the restoration of exiles; Alexander arranged the order in which they would be received.

l: Olympias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. XII. /
s: Olympias envied Hephaestion and accused and threatened him in letters. Hephaestion replied with severe rebukes, asserting that Alexander would judge between them. She later quarreled with Antipater, and her accusations contributed to Alexander’s estrangement from him.

l: Sisygambis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. XII. /
s: Darius’s mother once mistakenly prostrated herself before Hephaestion, believing him to be Alexander. Alexander told her not to be troubled because Hephaestion was another Alexander.

l: Antipater, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. XII. /
s: Antipater was Alexander’s viceroy in Europe and quarreled with Olympias. According to the poisoning account, he ordered his son, who was Alexander’s cup-bearer, to put poison into Alexander’s wine.

l: Cassander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. XII. /
s: Cassander succeeded his father, Antipater, in the kingdom after Alexander’s death. He was described as a great enemy of Alexander’s interests, allowed Olympias’s murdered body to remain unburied, and worked to rebuild Thebes, which Alexander had destroyed.

l: Sysigambis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. XII. /
s: Sysigambis, the mother of Darius, mourned Alexander’s death with many tears and refused both food and light. She died of hunger on the fifth day, in extreme sorrow but with honor and reputation.

l: Babylon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. XII. /
s: Alexander entered Babylon despite the Chaldeans’ warnings and later became troubled by their predictions. While visiting the newly made harbor at Babylon, he was separated from the other ships and endured several days of danger before returning safely.

l: Alexander's funeral pile, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. XII. /
s: Alexander built Hephaestion’s funeral pile at Babylon after demolishing and removing the bricks from ten furlongs of the city wall. The square structure had sides one furlong long, thirty apartments, numerous decorated levels, and a total height of more than one hundred and thirty cubits.

l: Alexander's illness, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. XII. /
s: After drinking heavily at Medius’s banquet, Alexander gave a deep sigh and was carried to his bed. His illness worsened, his pain became severe, and the physicians could not provide relief; he eventually despaired of life and gave his ring to Perdiccas.

l: Alexander's poisoning theory, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. XII. /
s: Some writers claimed that Alexander died from a deadly potion rather than from illness. They attributed the alleged poisoning to Antipater, who supposedly ordered his cup-bearer son to put poison in Alexander’s wine, although the account notes that some historians may have avoided reporting this because of Antipater’s power and Cassander’s succession.

l: prodigies foretelling Alexander's death, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. XII. /
s: The extinguishing of the Persian Holy Fire during Hephaestion’s funeral was regarded as an omen of Alexander’s death. Other prodigies included a chained man putting on Alexander’s robes and crown and sitting on his throne, and Alexander’s diadem being lost in the water and later recovered by a sailor; diviners interpreted these events as warnings and advised sacrifices.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVIII.
s: After Alexander the Macedonian died without issue, a succession crisis arose, and Aridaeus, the son of Philip, was made king under the name Philip. Perdiccas received executive authority, while Alexander's commanders were assigned governorships across the empire. Perdiccas ordered the execution of Meleager and other turbulent soldiers, and the Macedonians rejected Alexander's costly plans recorded in his notebooks. The Greeks in the upper provinces revolted under Python's command against them, but the Macedonians ultimately broke their capitulation and killed them all.

l: Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVIII.
s: Alexander's death left the government without a head and caused disputes over the succession. His notebooks contained plans for a Carthaginian expedition, a coastal road in Africa, magnificent temples, naval bases, new colonies, population transfers between Asia and Europe, and a monument for Philip; the Macedonians judged these projects impracticable and set them aside.

l: Aridaeus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVIII.
s: Aridaeus, the son of Philip and a man described as weak-spirited and afflicted by natural infirmities, was made king after Alexander's death.

l: king Philip, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVIII.
s: Philip III was the name given to Aridaeus when he was made king. He summoned a general council of the chief commanders, while Perdiccas exercised the executive power.

l: Perdiccas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVIII.
s: Perdiccas received Alexander's ring and was invested with the executive power of the kingdom under Philip III. He referred Alexander's costly plans to a general council, ordered the execution of thirty turbulent soldiers, privately caused Meleager to be executed, and sent Python against the revolting Greeks.

l: Meleager, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVIII.
s: Meleager was the leading figure among the phalanx and encouraged the Macedonian foot soldiers to oppose the commanders' party. He helped carry on the mutiny and was later executed by Perdiccas.

l: Python, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVIII.
s: Python, a former squire of Alexander and a skilled commander, was chosen general against the revolting Greeks. He intended to win them over and use their forces to establish his own power, but Perdiccas ordered him to put them all to the sword; after the Macedonians killed the Greeks despite their capitulation, Python returned to Perdiccas.

l: Macedonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVIII.
s: The Macedonians' foot soldiers initially supported Aridaeus, while the commanders and the Social Horse opposed them, but both sides agreed to make Aridaeus king and Perdiccas executive authority. They rejected Alexander's costly projects as impracticable and, after Python defeated the revolting Greeks and granted them safe conduct, suddenly attacked and killed them.

l: Greeks in the upper provinces, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVIII.
s: The Greeks in the upper provinces had endured being sent to the remote parts of Alexander's kingdom while he lived. After his death, they sought to return home, chose Python as their captain, assembled more than twenty thousand infantry and three thousand cavalry, and were ultimately killed by the Macedonians after their defeat.

l: Alexander's captains, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVIII.
s: Alexander's commanders and the king's bodyguards participated in the settlement of the succession and were made responsible for governing the provinces under the authority of the king and Perdiccas. They received assignments including Egypt, Syria, Cilicia, Media, Cappadocia, Phrygia, Lydia, Caria, Macedonia, and other regions.

l: Greek revolt in the upper provinces, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVIII.
s: The Greek revolt in the upper provinces began after Alexander's death, when the Greeks sought to escape their exile and return to Greece. Perdiccas sent Python against it with Macedonian troops and reinforcements from the provincial governors; the revolt was defeated, and its participants were killed.

l: Alexander's death, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVIII.
s: Alexander's death occurred without issue and left the government without a head, producing disputes and divisions over the succession. It also prompted the revolt of the Greeks in the upper provinces and led to the abandonment of his costly proposed projects.

l: succession crisis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVIII.
s: The succession crisis followed Alexander's death without issue. The infantry supported Aridaeus, while leading nobles, bodyguards, and the Social Horse prepared to oppose the Macedonian phalanx; the dispute was settled by making Aridaeus king as Philip III and Perdiccas executive authority.

l: division of the provinces, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVIII.
s: The division of the provinces placed Egypt under Ptolemy, Syria under Laomedon, Cilicia under Philotas, Media under Pithon, Cappadocia and Paphlagonia under Eumenes, Lycia and Greater Phrygia under Antigonus, Caria under Cassander, Lydia under Meleager, and other territories under various commanders. Macedonia and the neighboring regions were assigned to Antipater, while Lysimachus received Thrace and the areas bordering the Pontus.

l: Asia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVIII.
s: Asia is described as divided by a continuous mountain range extending from Taurus in Cilicia to Caucasus and the eastern ocean. Its northern and southern provinces, rivers, climates, and major regions, including India, Persia, Babylon, Mesopotamia, Syria, and the coastal countries, are surveyed to clarify the geography of the subsequent events.

l: Babylon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVIII.
s: Babylon was the place where Alexander died and where the succession settlement was made. Its province was assigned to Archon, while Mesopotamia was assigned to Arcesilaus.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, la the mean time, in Europe, the Rhodkns east out the garrison of
s: After Alexander ordered the restoration of many Greek exiles, the Athenians and Aetolians opposed the measure and later declared war against Antipater, beginning the Lamian War. Athens organized a Greek alliance, raised forces under Leosthenes, and proclaimed that it would defend the common liberty of Greece and remove Macedonian garrisons. Leosthenes defeated the Boeotians and then forced Antipater to retreat into Lamia, where the Macedonians withstood a siege until Leosthenes was mortally wounded. After Leosthenes’s death, Antiphilus was appointed commander, while Craterus was summoned from Cilicia with Macedonian reinforcements.

Eumenes strengthened his forces there with cavalry raised from his own province.

s: Alexander's body was carried from Babylon toward Egypt in a highly elaborate funeral procession. Ptolemy built a temple in Alexandria for the body and honored Alexander with sacrifices and magnificent spectacles.

l: Aridaeus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IIL
s: Aridssus spent two years preparing Alexander's funeral chariot and brought Alexander's body from Babylon toward Egypt.

l: Ptolemy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IIL
s: Ptolemy met Alexander's body with his army as far as Syria, received it, and accompanied it with great care. He kept the body in Alexandria, built a temple for it, and honored Alexander with sacrifices and magnificent spectacles.

l: Perdiccas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IIL
s: Perdiccas suspected Ptolemy's growing power and prepared to lead the kings and his army on an expedition into Egypt against him. He gave Eumenes troops and officers and ordered him to march to the Hellespont to prevent Antipater and Craterus from crossing into Asia.

l: Eumenes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IIL
s: Eumenes received a considerable force from Perdiccas and marched to the Hellespont. He completed his army with cavalry raised from his own province, since his troops had previously lacked sufficient horse.

l: Neoptolemus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IIL
s: Neoptolemus was one of the illustrious commanders placed under Eumenes's authority and was ordered to obey him in all things.

l: Craterus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IIL
s: Craterus was associated with Antipater, whose passage into Asia Eumenes was ordered to prevent.

l: Macedonian kings, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IIL
s: Perdiccas intended to take the kings with him on his expedition into Egypt against Ptolemy.

l: the army of Perdiccas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IIL
s: The army of Perdiccas was being prepared for war against Ptolemy in Egypt. Perdiccas assigned part of it, with officers, to Eumenes for operations at the Hellespont.

l: Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IIL
s: Egypt was the destination of Perdiccas's planned expedition against Ptolemy. Alexander's body was brought to Egypt, though Ptolemy kept it in Alexandria rather than sending it to the temple of Ammon.

l: Hellespont, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IIL
s: The Hellespont was the place to which Eumenes marched with his assigned forces. He was ordered to prevent Antipater and Craterus from crossing it into Asia.

l: Alexandria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IIL
s: Alexandria, the city Alexander had built, became the place where Ptolemy deposited Alexander's body. Ptolemy built a temple there in Alexander's honor.

l: Alexander's funeral chariot, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IIL
s: Alexander's funeral chariot was constructed with exceptional expense, magnificence, and workmanship. It included a gold coffin and cover, a decorated arch, images, tables portraying Alexander's achievements, gold-covered wheels, and sixty-four richly adorned mules.

l: Alexander's body, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IIL
s: Alexander's body was placed in a gold coffin filled partly with aromatic spices to preserve it. Aridssus brought it from Babylon toward Egypt, and Ptolemy received it in Syria and placed it in Alexandria.

l: the funeral procession, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IIL
s: The funeral procession attracted crowds from every city through which it passed, and spectators followed it to view the chariot. Workmen and pioneers accompanied it to level and smooth the roads.

l: the wars of the Successors, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IIL
s: The wars of the Successors are represented here by Perdiccas's planned war against Ptolemy in Egypt and by the effort to prevent Antipater and Craterus from crossing into Asia.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, But after Antipater and Craterus had transported their army out
s: After Antipater and Craterus transported their army out of Europe, Neoptolemus's treachery against Eumenes was discovered, and Eumenes defeated him, causing many Macedonians to join Eumenes's army. Antipater and Craterus divided their forces, but Eumenes defeated Craterus's army in Cappadocia, killing Craterus and Neoptolemus. Perdiccas then invaded Egypt, but his assault and attempted crossing of the Nile failed, leading his soldiers and commanders to turn against him and kill him. Ptolemy gained the Macedonians' favor, while Eumenes was condemned by them after news of his victory arrived.

l: Antipater, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, But after Antipater and Craterus had transported their army out
s: After transporting his army out of Europe, Antipater received Neoptolemus, who had fled to him with three hundred horse. He and Craterus divided their army so that Antipater would march into Cilicia against Perdiccas while Craterus fought Eumenes; after Craterus's defeat, Antipater hastened to Cilicia.

l: Craterus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, But after Antipater and Craterus had transported their army out
s: Craterus took command of the force sent against Eumenes and promised his soldiers the field's pillage if they won. He commanded the right wing, but was thrown from his horse during the battle, trampled without being recognized, and killed.

l: Neoptolemus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, But after Antipater and Craterus had transported their army out
s: Neoptolemus secretly joined with Antipater against Eumenes, but his treachery was discovered and he lost almost all his men. He later commanded the left wing against Eumenes, fought him hand to hand, and was killed by a blow to the neck after Eumenes hamstrung him.

l: Eumenes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, But after Antipater and Craterus had transported their army out
s: Eumenes defeated Neoptolemus, incorporated the surviving Macedonians into his army, and collected many horsemen because he lacked infantry able to confront the Macedonian phalanx. In the battle against Craterus's army, he defeated both wings, killed Neoptolemus, retained the field and the bodies of both commanders, and sent terms to the phalanx. He was wounded and could not effectively pursue the Macedonians when they broke their oath and departed, but news of his victory later led the Macedonians to condemn him and his adherents to death.

l: Perdiccas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, But after Antipater and Craterus had transported their army out
s: Perdiccas marched into Egypt after hearing of Eumenes's victory, but the Nile defeated his works and his assault on a fort failed. During an attempted crossing, the river swept away many of his soldiers, more than two thousand perished, and his army became disaffected. His commanders and soldiers turned against him, and a group of horsemen killed him after he had held sovereign command for three years.

l: Ptolemy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, But after Antipater and Craterus had transported their army out
s: Ptolemy defended the Egyptian fort against Perdiccas, personally fought on the bulwark, wounded an elephant and its Indian driver, and encouraged his followers. He treated the bodies of Perdiccas's dead soldiers with funeral rites and returned their ashes and bones to their relatives, winning the affection of the Macedonians. Although he could have sought the protectorship of the kings, he advised that Python and Aridaeus receive the command instead.

l: Macedonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, But after Antipater and Craterus had transported their army out
s: Macedonian soldiers joined Eumenes after his victory over Neoptolemus but later broke their oath, reassembled, and secretly departed to Antipater. Perdiccas's Macedonian troops became hostile to him after the Nile disaster, while Ptolemy's treatment of the dead won their affection. After Perdiccas's death, they appointed Python and Aridaeus protectors of the kings and condemned Eumenes and his adherents to death.

l: the army under Antipater and Craterus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, But after Antipater and Craterus had transported their army out
s: After leaving Europe, this army was divided into two bodies: Antipater led one toward Cilicia against Perdiccas, while Craterus led the other against Eumenes. Craterus's portion was defeated in Cappadocia, and after Craterus's death and the breaking of both wings, the surviving horsemen withdrew to the phalanx.

l: Eumenes's army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, But after Antipater and Craterus had transported their army out
s: Eumenes's army was reinforced by Macedonians who remained after the defeat of Neoptolemus. It included about twenty-eight thousand infantry from different nations and five thousand horse, on whose strength Eumenes chiefly relied against Craterus's force.

l: Macedonian phalanx, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, But after Antipater and Craterus had transported their army out
s: The phalanx served as a place of refuge for the defeated horsemen after both wings were broken. Eumenes offered its soldiers the choice of joining him or departing, and although they swore fidelity and received permission to obtain provisions, they secretly reassembled and went to Antipater.

l: Cilicia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, But after Antipater and Craterus had transported their army out
s: Cilicia was the destination of Antipater's march after the army was divided, where he intended to fight Perdiccas. Antipater hastened there after receiving the survivors of Craterus's defeat.

l: Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, But after Antipater and Craterus had transported their army out
s: Egypt was the territory invaded by Perdiccas and defended by Ptolemy. Perdiccas's expedition there failed after the Nile damaged his works, his assault on a fort was repulsed, and his army suffered heavy losses while crossing the river.

l: Cappadocia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, But after Antipater and Craterus had transported their army out
s: Cappadocia was the place where Eumenes defeated the force commanded by Craterus and Neoptolemus. News of this victory reached the Macedonians after Perdiccas's death.

l: Nile, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, But after Antipater and Craterus had transported their army out
s: The Nile overflowed while Perdiccas was cleansing an old sluice, ruined his works, and later created severe difficulties for his army's crossing. Its current and shifting sand caused many soldiers to drown or be carried away, while others were captured or devoured by crocodiles.

l: the battle between Eumenes and Craterus's army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, But after Antipater and Craterus had transported their army out
s: In this battle, the horse on both sides advanced ahead of the infantry. Craterus was killed, Eumenes killed Neoptolemus in single combat, both enemy wings were broken, and Eumenes held the field before allowing the surviving Macedonians to depart.

l: Perdiccas's Egyptian expedition, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, But after Antipater and Craterus had transported their army out
s: Perdiccas's expedition began with confidence after he heard of Eumenes's victory, but it was hindered by the Nile and by Ptolemy's defense of a fort. A failed river crossing caused more than two thousand deaths and turned the army and commanders against Perdiccas.

l: Perdiccas's death, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, But after Antipater and Craterus had transported their army out
s: Perdiccas's death occurred after his failed Egyptian operations and the Nile disaster. Disaffected commanders and soldiers conspired against him, and horsemen entered his tent and killed him; afterward, Python and Aridaeus were appointed protectors of the kings.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, . • After Antipater had gonfe over into Asia, the iEtolians, in pursu-
s: The unit describes the Aetolians' invasion of Thessaly, their withdrawal to defend Aetolia, and Polyperchon's defeat of their forces under Menon of Pharsalia. At Triparadisus, Antipater became protector with absolute authority and made a new division of the provinces, assigning commands throughout Asia. Antigonus then defeated Eumenes in Cappadocia, forcing him and about six hundred loyal followers to take refuge in the stronghold of Nora. Meanwhile, Ptolemy conquered Syria and Phoenicia from Egypt, while Antigonus's growing power threatened Antipater and the kings.

l: Antipater, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, . • After Antipater had gonfe over into Asia, the iEtolians, in pursu-
s: After going into Asia, Antipater's general Polycles was defeated and killed by the Aetolians. At Triparadisus, the Macedonians chose Antipater protector with absolute authority; he later quieted a mutiny stirred up by Eurydice and made a second division of the provinces.

l: Aetolians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, . • After Antipater had gonfe over into Asia, the iEtolians, in pursu-
s: The Aetolians entered Thessaly with twelve thousand foot and four thousand horse under Alexander, besieged Amphissa, ravaged Locrian territory, and defeated Polycles. They gained Thessalian support, but withdrew most of their forces under Menon of Pharsalia when the Acarnanians invaded Aetolia; Polyperchon then defeated Menon and recovered Thessaly.

l: Perdiccas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, . • After Antipater had gonfe over into Asia, the iEtolians, in pursu-
s: Perdiccas, a chief commander of Eumenes, deserted with three thousand foot and five hundred horse. Eumenes sent Phenices against him, captured him and his followers, and put the chief leaders of the defection to death.

l: Thessaly, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, . • After Antipater had gonfe over into Asia, the iEtolians, in pursu-
s: The Aetolians entered Thessaly and persuaded many inhabitants to join their war against Antipater. Polyperchon later defeated the Aetolian forces there and soon recovered the province.

l: Aetolia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, . • After Antipater had gonfe over into Asia, the iEtolians, in pursu-
s: While the Aetolians were campaigning in Thessaly, the Acarnanians invaded Aetolia, wasted and spoiled its country, and besieged its cities. The Aetolians returned with their own soldiers and so frightened the Acarnanians that they relieved the country.

l: Menon of Pharsalia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, . • After Antipater had gonfe over into Asia, the iEtolians, in pursu-
s: Menon of Pharsalia was left in Thessaly in command of the Aetolian forces. Polyperchon fought and routed him, killed him, and cut off most of his army.

l: Polyperchon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, . • After Antipater had gonfe over into Asia, the iEtolians, in pursu-
s: Polyperchon, left as general in Macedonia, entered Thessaly with a strong army. He defeated the Aetolian forces under Menon of Pharsalia, killed Menon, and recovered Thessaly.

l: Macedonia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, . • After Antipater had gonfe over into Asia, the iEtolians, in pursu-
s: Polyperchon was left as general in Macedonia while Antipater went to Triparadisus and later marched toward Macedonia with the kings and his troops.

l: Aridaeus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, . • After Antipater had gonfe over into Asia, the iEtolians, in pursu-
s: Aridaeus was one of the protectors of the kings and came from the Nile with the kings and the army to Triparadisus. He is also identified as the husband of Eurydice, one of the kings of Macedon.

l: Python, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, . • After Antipater had gonfe over into Asia, the iEtolians, in pursu-
s: Python was a protector of the kings who became dissatisfied with Eurydice's interference. He and his friends gave up the protectorship, after which the Macedonians chose Antipater; a separate Python, son of Agenor, was assigned India bordering Paropamisus.

l: Macedonian kings, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, . • After Antipater had gonfe over into Asia, the iEtolians, in pursu-
s: The kings came with Aridaeus, Python, and the army from the Nile to Triparadisus. Antipater later marched with them toward Macedonia to conduct them back into their own country, while Antigonus was appointed commander of the royal army.

l: Triparadisus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, . • After Antipater had gonfe over into Asia, the iEtolians, in pursu-
s: At Triparadisus in Higher Syria, Aridaeus and Python gave up the protectorship after conflict with Eurydice. The Macedonians then chose Antipater protector with absolute authority, and Antipater subsequently made a second division of the provinces there.

l: Eurydice, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, . • After Antipater had gonfe over into Asia, the iEtolians, in pursu-
s: Eurydice interfered in matters of government and tried to control the protectors, causing Python and his friends to become disgusted. At Triparadisus she stirred the Macedonians to mutiny against Antipater, but he calmed the army and brought her to a more moderate temper.

l: Macedonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, . • After Antipater had gonfe over into Asia, the iEtolians, in pursu-
s: The Macedonians were described as more attentive to Eurydice's commands than to those of the protectors. They chose Antipater as protector with absolute authority, later mutinied under Eurydice's influence, and were calmed by Antipater's arguments.

l: division of the provinces, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, . • After Antipater had gonfe over into Asia, the iEtolians, in pursu-
s: Antipater made a second division of the provinces after the events at Triparadisus. Ptolemy retained Egypt, Laomedon received Syria, Seleucus received Babylon, Antigonus received Susiana and the Greater Phrygia and Cilicia, and other commanders received the remaining provinces listed in the account.

l: Ptolemy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, . • After Antipater had gonfe over into Asia, the iEtolians, in pursu-
s: Ptolemy retained Egypt because he had gained it as a conqueror. He later sent Nicanor into Syria and took Laomedon prisoner, bringing Syria and the cities of Phoenicia under his power before returning to Egypt.

l: Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, . • After Antipater had gonfe over into Asia, the iEtolians, in pursu-
s: Egypt remained under Ptolemy, who possessed it as a conqueror. From Egypt he sought to take Phoenicia and Coele-Syria and ultimately brought Syria and Phoenicia under his power.

l: Syria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, . • After Antipater had gonfe over into Asia, the iEtolians, in pursu-
s: Antipater assigned Syria to Laomedon of Mitylene. Ptolemy sent Nicanor against it, captured Laomedon, and brought all Syria under his own power.

l: Antigonus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, . • After Antipater had gonfe over into Asia, the iEtolians, in pursu-
s: Antigonus was rewarded with Susiana because he had first caused the overthrow of Perdiccas and was appointed commander of the royal army. He defeated Eumenes in Cappadocia, besieged him at Nora, and began aspiring to greater power while secretly resolving not to remain subordinate to Antipater or the kings.

l: Cappadocia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, . • After Antipater had gonfe over into Asia, the iEtolians, in pursu-
s: Eumenes was in Cappadocia when Perdiccas deserted him. Antigonus later fought Eumenes there, defeated him, and forced him to take refuge in Nora.

l: royal army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, . • After Antipater had gonfe over into Asia, the iEtolians, in pursu-
s: Antigonus was appointed general of the royal army and ordered to pursue and destroy Eumenes. The royal army was also said to be necessary for dispossessing Porus and Taxiles from their kingdoms.

l: Eumenes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, . • After Antipater had gonfe over into Asia, the iEtolians, in pursu-
s: Eumenes captured Perdiccas and his army after a night attack and spared most of the ordinary soldiers, incorporating them into his own forces. Antigonus later defeated him in Cappadocia, after which Eumenes withdrew to Nora with about six hundred loyal followers and continued negotiating and preparing for possible changes in fortune.

l: Nora, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, . • After Antipater had gonfe over into Asia, the iEtolians, in pursu-
s: Nora was a small but impregnable fort in Cappadocia, built on a high rock and supplied with provisions for many years. Eumenes and about six hundred followers took refuge there after his defeat, and Antigonus blockaded it with walls, trenches, and earthworks.

l: battle in Cappadocia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, . • After Antipater had gonfe over into Asia, the iEtolians, in pursu-
s: Antigonus and Eumenes fought a sharp battle in Cappadocia. Antigonus won after Apollonides deserted Eumenes with his horse, killed eight thousand of the enemy, and captured their baggage and carriages.

l: Phoenicia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, . • After Antipater had gonfe over into Asia, the iEtolians, in pursu-
s: Ptolemy sought to possess the cities of Phoenicia because the region lay conveniently near Egypt. Nicanor took its cities and placed garrisons in them before returning to Egypt.

l: Coele-Syria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, . • After Antipater had gonfe over into Asia, the iEtolians, in pursu-
s: Ptolemy sought to possess Coele-Syria along with Phoenicia because of its convenient position near Egypt. The account states that Nicanor brought Syria and the cities of Phoenicia under Ptolemy's power.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: Antigonus defeated Alcetas in Pisidia, captured many of his commanders, and forced Alcetas to seek refuge in Termessus, where Alcetas was betrayed and killed himself. Antigonus then pursued wider control in Asia, confronting Aridaeus, seizing money intended for the kings, and attempting to remove provincial governors. After Antipater’s death, Polyperchon became protector of the kings in Macedonia, while Cassander plotted to displace him and Antigonus pursued sovereignty. Eumenes, previously defeated and besieged by Antigonus, was released after agreeing to cooperate with him and soon began rebuilding his forces.

l: Antigonus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: Antigonus marched from Cappadocia into Pisidia, defeated Alcetas, captured several commanders, and absorbed many prisoners into his army. After Alcetas’s death, he dishonored and abandoned his body, then pursued wider power in Asia by opposing Aridaeus, seizing money intended for the kings, and attempting to remove provincial governors. He also released Eumenes from the siege of Nora after securing his cooperation.

l: Alcetas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: Alcetas was defeated by Antigonus in Pisidia and escaped with his life-guard, children, and Pisidian supporters to Termessus. When the elders of Termessus betrayed him, he killed himself rather than be captured, and the young men of the city later buried his abused body.

l: Eumenes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: Eumenes had earlier been defeated by Antigonus and confined for a year in Nora. Antigonus later made an agreement with him and released him, after which Eumenes gathered former friends and soldiers and began rebuilding a force in support of the kings.

l: Perdiccas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: Perdiccas is described as dead before the events of this unit. Alcetas and Attalus remained among the last of his friends and kindred capable of opposing Antigonus.

l: Antipater, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: Antipater died after appointing Polyperchon protector of the kings with chief authority and Cassander as chiliarch. Before his death, he ordered the execution of Demeas, son and fellow ambassador of Demades, because letters connected Demeas with opposition to him.

l: Polyperchon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: Polyperchon succeeded Antipater as protector of the kings and received chief and absolute authority in Macedonia. He invited Olympias from Epirus to care for Alexander’s son and rule as queen-regent, and he opposed Cassander’s ambitions.

l: Cassander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: Cassander resented Polyperchon’s appointment and considered it dishonorable that supreme authority should pass to someone outside his family. He secretly gathered supporters, sought alliances with Ptolemy and others, and plotted to obtain the chief command.

l: Olympias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: Olympias had withdrawn to Epirus because of her quarrels with Antipater. Polyperchon invited her to return to Macedonia, care for Alexander’s son, and reside there as queen-regent.

l: Aridaeus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: Aridaeus, governor of Phrygia at the Hellespont, fortified his principal cities and besieged Cyzicum. After the siege failed, he refused Antigonus’s demand that he leave the province and declared that he would settle the dispute by force.

l: Pisidia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: Pisidia was the site of Antigonus’s campaign against Alcetas. After Alcetas’s defeat and death, Antigonus left the region, while young men of Termessus continued raiding territory associated with Antigonus.

l: Cappadocia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: Cappadocia was the region from which Antigonus marched against Alcetas. Eumenes had previously ruled Cappadocia prosperously and later remained there briefly after his release from Nora.

l: Termessus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: Termessus sheltered Alcetas after his defeat. Its elders secretly betrayed him to Antigonus, while its young men resisted the betrayal, later buried Alcetas, and ravaged territory connected with Antigonus.

l: Macedonia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: Macedonia became the center of the succession dispute after Antipater’s death. Polyperchon was appointed protector of the kings there, while Cassander plotted to displace him and Polyperchon sought Olympias’s return.

l: Asia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: Asia was unsettled after Antipater’s death as its commanders pursued their own interests. Antigonus, strengthened by his victories and large army, aimed to control its provinces, remove their governors, and establish himself as sovereign.

l: Cyzicum, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: Cyzicum resisted Aridaeus despite being surprised and initially unable to defend itself. Its inhabitants secretly armed the city, obtained help from Byzantium, recovered people trapped outside the walls, and forced Aridaeus to abandon the siege.

l: siege of Cyzicum, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: Aridaeus began the siege of Cyzicum with a large force and siege equipment, but the city’s defenders deceived him while preparing their defenses. Assistance from Byzantium and control of the sea enabled Cyzicum to defeat the besiegers and compel Aridaeus to withdraw; Antigonus arrived too late to relieve it.
